title: Pediatric Cataract -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Pediatric cataracts represent a significant cause of preventable childhood visual impairment and blindness, necessitating early detection and timely intervention to support normal visual development. Presentation commonly includes leukocoria, strabismus, and nystagmus. Cataracts may be congenital, arising from genetic abnormalities or prenatal factors such as intrauterine infection, or acquired postnatally because of trauma, metabolic disease, or inflammatory conditions. Risk factors include family history, prematurity, systemic syndromes, and exposure to intrauterine toxins. Opacification of the crystalline lens interferes with visual pathway maturation and may lead to amblyopia and irreversible cortical visual deficits if treatment is delayed. Evaluation requires careful differentiation from other causes of leukocoria through comprehensive examination and appropriate imaging. Management strategies depend on etiology and severity and may include surgical extraction, optical rehabilitation, and long-term amblyopia therapy. Visual prognosis is closely linked to the timing of intervention, cataract density, and adherence to follow-up care.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This educational activity enhances clinician competence in the evaluation and management of pediatric cataracts across the continuum of care. Participants develop a deeper understanding of disease etiology, pathophysiology, diagnostic approaches, and evidence-based treatment strategies, including postoperative visual rehabilitation. Instruction emphasizes risk assessment, interpretation of diagnostic findings, and anticipation of complications such as glaucoma and posterior capsule opacification. Collaboration within an interprofessional team, including pediatric specialists, optometrists, genetic counselors, and rehabilitation professionals, supports coordinated care, improves adherence to therapy, and optimizes long-term visual outcomes for affected children.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Introduction
content: Pediatric cataracts are a leading cause of treatable childhood blindness. Delayed recognition and treatment are associated with substantial social, economic, and emotional consequences at the individual, familial, and community levels. Effective management remains challenging because prevention of irreversible amblyopia depends on early identification, timely diagnosis, and prompt intervention. [1]

content: Population-based vision screening programs and caregiver recognition of early signs, such as leukocoria and strabismus, facilitate timely diagnosis and treatment. title: Pediatric Cataract -- Introduction
content: Globally, pediatric cataracts constitute a major cause of preventable childhood blindness, particularly in low- and middle-income regions, where delayed diagnosis frequently results in advanced clinical presentations, including nystagmus, poor fixation, and dense lens opacities. Early surgical intervention is associated with improved visual outcomes, enhanced functional development, and reduced long-term socioeconomic burden. Pediatric cataracts account for approximately 5% to 20% of childhood blindness and severe visual impairment worldwide, with an estimated incidence of 1.8 to 3.6 per 10,000 children per year and a prevalence ranging from 1 to 15 per 10,000 children. [5]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Introduction
content: Hereditary congenital cataracts have a prevalence of 8.3% and 25%, with approximately 75% of cases following an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. Pathogenic variants in crystallin proteins, which are essential for maintaining lens transparency and refractive function, have been associated with several cataract subtypes, including nuclear, lamellar, zonular, and posterior polar. Nonsyndromic inherited cataracts frequently involve genetic alterations in crystallin or connexin genes. PITX3 mutations are specifically linked to posterior polar cataracts, while PAX6 alterations are associated with anterior polar cataracts. [8]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Introduction
content: Syndromic cataracts are linked to specific genetic defects, including α-galactosidase A in Fabry disease, galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase ( GALT ) in galactosemia, OCRL in Lowe (oculocerebrorenal) syndrome, and NHS in Nance–Horan syndrome, a cataract–dental disorder (see Image . Congenital Cataracts and Abnormal Galactose Metabolism). Maternal and congenital infections, particularly Toxoplasma gondii , rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, and Treponema pallidum (syphilis)—collectively known as TORCH pathogens—are also major contributors to pediatric cataracts. B Mahalakshmi et al reported a high prevalence of TORCH infections in the Indian subcontinent, with 20% of cases testing seropositive. Ocular trauma is another significant cause, accounting for 12% to 46% of pediatric cataract cases. [9]

content: Concerns exist regarding the higher incidence of complications, such as glaucoma, uveitis, dense posterior capsule opacification, and increased secondary interventions following primary IOL implantation in children younger than 2. [10] Primary IOL implantation in this age group has nevertheless demonstrated safety, with excellent long-term outcomes compared to aphakia and secondary IOL implantation after age 2. The myopic shift is generally well controlled; visual acuity outcomes are favorable; and the incidence of complications, such as glaucoma, uveitis, membrane formation, synechiae, and the need for secondary interventions, is lower than previously reported. Special care is necessary for infants younger than 6 months because of the increased risk of adverse events in smaller eyes. [11]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Introduction
content: The process of emmetropisation in children is typically complete by age 12, with axial length increasing from approximately 16.5 mm at birth to 23 mm by age 13. This growth proceeds in 3 phases: rapid (0.46 mm/month from birth to 6 months), infantile (0.15 mm/month from 6 to 18 months), and juvenile (0.15 mm/month from 18 months to 12 years). Corneal curvature also changes significantly, with mean keratometry readings decreasing from approximately 51.2 D at birth to 43.5 D in adulthood. Consequently, IOL power selection in pediatric patients must account for axial elongation and the associated myopic shift. This consideration necessitates the use of pediatric-specific IOL power calculation formulas adapted for ongoing ocular growth. Sharp-edged IOLs are now widely preferred due to an association with lower rates of visual axis opacification (VAO). Compared with round-edged lenses, sharp-edged designs result in fewer neodymium-doped yttrium aluminum garnet laser capsulotomies, occurring in 1 of 371 eyes compared with 4 of 371 eyes.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Introduction
content: Prompt management of pediatric cataracts is essential for optimal visual development. Most children with congenital or developmental cataracts require surgical intervention. Initial assessment of visual significance may be performed using the red reflex during distant direct ophthalmoscopy (see Image . Red Reflex). For visually significant cataracts, bilateral cases should be treated between 6 and 8 weeks of age, while unilateral cases require earlier intervention, typically between 4 and 6 weeks. [12]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Etiology -- Classification of Pediatric Cataracts by Etiology and Systemic Association
content: Pediatric cataracts arise from a wide spectrum of underlying conditions, with laterality, associated systemic findings, and clinical context providing key clues to the underlying cause. Below is an overview of common causes encountered in clinical practice, emphasizing patterns relevant to diagnosis and management. Genetic or hereditary pediatric cataracts result from autosomal-dominant mutations in CRYAA , CRYBB2 , GJA8 , and MIP , as well as from autosomal-recessive or X-linked forms.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Etiology -- Classification of Pediatric Cataracts by Etiology and Systemic Association
content: These cataracts are frequently bilateral, often isolated, and may be associated with microphthalmia or other ocular anomalies. Metabolic disorders, such as galactosemia caused by GALT deficiency, galactokinase deficiency, hypocalcemia or hypoparathyroidism, and diabetes mellitus, can produce characteristic lens opacities, including the “oil droplet” or snowflake cataract. These cases are often bilateral, accompanied by systemic manifestations, and require urgent metabolic management, particularly in galactosemia. Cataracts associated with intrauterine or perinatal infections, ie, TORCH, may coexist with microcephaly, sensorineural deafness, or chorioretinitis. Opacities are often bilateral in rubella.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Etiology -- Classification of Pediatric Cataracts by Etiology and Systemic Association
content: Pediatric cataracts may arise in the context of systemic syndromes, including Down syndrome, in which cerulean cataracts are observed. Marfan syndrome is often associated with ectopia lentis, with or without cataract. Lowe syndrome, Nance–Horan syndrome, and myotonic dystrophy are also implicated. Cataracts in these conditions are frequently accompanied by multisystem manifestations and may represent the presenting feature. Ocular developmental abnormalities, such as persistent fetal vasculature, aniridia, microphthalmia, and posterior or anterior lenticonus, typically present unilaterally and may necessitate early surgical intervention due to visual axis distortion.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Etiology -- Classification of Pediatric Cataracts by Etiology and Systemic Association
content: Trauma, including blunt trauma resulting in rosette cataract, penetrating injuries, and birth trauma (eg, forceps), represents the most common cause of unilateral pediatric cataract. Iatrogenic cataracts may occur following ocular surgery, such as vitrectomy, or secondary to steroid therapy, often manifesting as posterior subcapsular opacities. Therapeutic radiation, commonly administered in oncology patients, produces dose-dependent posterior subcapsular cataracts. Drug-induced lens opacities result from prolonged exposure to systemic corticosteroids, chlorpromazine, or, rarely, amiodarone. Idiopathic cataracts, ie, those without identifiable cause after complete evaluation, account for approximately 25% to 30% of pediatric cases. Pattern differences should be noted during patient evaluation. Most bilateral cataracts arise from genetic, metabolic, syndromic, or infectious causes, while unilateral cataracts generally result from trauma or developmental anomalies. Urgent evaluation is indicated for suspected galactosemia, TORCH infections, and syndromic associations. [20]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Epidemiology
content: Various epidemiological studies have been conducted to evaluate the causes of childhood blindness. Untreated pediatric cataracts account for approximately 7.4% to 15.3% of cases, with a higher burden in low-resource settings due to delayed diagnosis and access barriers. The incidence and prevalence of pediatric cataracts vary by region, with lower rates in high-income countries and higher rates in low-income settings. Incidence ranges from 1.8 to 3.6 per 10,000 children annually, while prevalence ranges from 0.63 to 13.6 per 10,000 in low-income countries such as Bangladesh, Pakistan, and India, compared to 0.42 to 2.05 per 10,000 in high-income countries such as the US and the UK. [21] No significant differences in prevalence have been observed based on sex or laterality. [22]

If not promptly treated, the condition can result in severe visual impairment, affecting the child's quality of life and placing socioeconomic strain on the family and broader community. Pediatric cataracts account for an estimated 5% to 20% of childhood blindness and severe visual impairment worldwide. The global incidence ranges from 1.8 to 3.6 per 10,000 children annually, and prevalence is estimated at 1 to 15 per 10,000. Country-specific studies show varied prevalence rates. In the US, the prevalence is estimated at 3 to 4 visually significant cataracts per 10,000 live births. [23]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Epidemiology
content: The prevalence of pediatric cataracts in the UK is approximately 3.18 per 10,000 live births. In China, the incidence is around 5 per 10,000 births. Although geographic variations in prevalence exist, significant differences in laterality (ie, whether 1 or both eyes are affected) or sex are not commonly reported. Hereditary cataracts account for approximately 30% of all pediatric cases, with about 75% following an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern and the remainder inherited in an autosomal recessive or X-linked fashion. Specific genetic conditions associated with pediatric cataracts include Down and Turner syndromes, as well as myotonic dystrophy. Several metabolic disorders also contribute to cataract development, including diabetes mellitus, hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, galactosemia, Fabry disease, Zellweger syndrome, hypoparathyroidism, and Lowe syndrome. [24]

Several metabolic disorders also contribute to cataract development, including diabetes mellitus, hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, galactosemia, Fabry disease, Zellweger syndrome, hypoparathyroidism, and Lowe syndrome. [24]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Epidemiology
content: Certain medications, such as steroids, miotics, chlorpromazine, and amiodarone, can induce cataracts in children, usually posterior subcapsular. Trauma is another major cause, accounting for 12% to 46% of pediatric cases and representing the leading cause of unilateral pediatric cataracts. Maternal and congenital infections, particularly those from the TORCHES group, are also notable contributors. A study conducted in the Indian subcontinent reported a high incidence of TORCH infections, with 20% of cases testing seropositive. Rubella remains a major cause of disease in regions with incomplete vaccination coverage.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Pathophysiology
content: Pediatric cataracts have diverse causes, including heritable genetic defects, fetal or childhood developmental insults, and associated systemic syndromes. Autosomal dominant inheritance is the most common pattern seen in hereditary cataracts. A genetic screening study conducted in Australia identified up to 51 genes and loci associated with the condition. [27] Crystallin mutations ( CRYAA, CRYAB ) cause nuclear or lamellar cataracts via protein aggregation, while connexin mutations ( GJA3, GJA8 ) lead to zonular cataracts from impaired metabolic coupling. Mutations in genes encoding transcription factors, such as PAX6 (anterior polar cataracts), FOXE3, MAF ( C-MAF ), PITX3 (posterior polar cataracts), MIP , and CRYAA , are frequently observed. Mutations in genes encoding crystallin and connexin are also common. [28] [29]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Pathophysiology
content: Pediatric cataracts cloud the eye's natural lens and impair vision. The multifactorial pathophysiology involves genetic, metabolic, infectious, and environmental factors that disrupt the lens's normal transparency and function. Genetic mutations contribute not only to the presence of pediatric cataracts but also to their phenotypic variability and severity. The affected genes encode proteins essential for lens structure, development, and transparency. Crystallins, for instance, are the primary structural proteins of the lens, maintaining its optical clarity and refractive index. Alterations in crystallin genes lead to protein misfolding or aggregation, resulting in distinct cataract morphologies, including nuclear, lamellar, zonular, and posterior polar types. Connexins form gap junctions that facilitate intercellular communication and metabolic balance within the lens. The disruption of these structures impairs homeostasis and contributes to lens opacification.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Pathophysiology
content: Pediatric cataracts may also arise from underlying metabolic disorders. Diabetes mellitus causes elevated blood glucose levels, leading to osmotic imbalances in the lens that result in swelling and vacuole formation, ultimately contributing to cataractogenesis (snowflake or diffuse cataracts). In galactosemia, accumulation of galactitol due to impaired galactose metabolism induces osmotic stress and leads to the formation of oil droplet cataracts. Hypocalcemia, characterized by low calcium levels, disrupts lens cell function and protein stability, promoting cataract formation. Fabry disease, a lysosomal storage disorder, is characterized by glycosphingolipid accumulation and is associated with spoke-like lens opacities. [30]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Pathophysiology
content: Maternal and congenital infections, particularly TORCH infections, can lead to congenital cataracts in newborns. These infections induce intrauterine inflammation and damage the developing lens, resulting in opacification. [31] Drug-induced cataracts may occur following prolonged exposure to specific medications. Corticosteroids, for instance, alter lens metabolism and protein structure, contributing to posterior subcapsular cataracts. Other drugs, such as miotics, chlorpromazine, and amiodarone, can induce lens opacities through oxidative stress or disruption of lens cell function. Trauma to the eye, whether accidental or intentional, can also result in cataract formation, ie, rosette or total cataracts from capsule breach and protein denaturation. [32]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Pathophysiology
content: Environmental and nutritional factors play significant roles in the development of pediatric cataracts. Prolonged exposure to UV radiation and other environmental stressors can heighten oxidative stress within the lens. This increased oxidative burden damages lens proteins and lipids, ultimately leading to cataract formation. Additionally, deficiencies in essential nutrients, particularly antioxidants such as vitamins C and E, can compromise lens health. Such deficiencies impair the lens’s ability to counteract oxidative damage and contribute to cataract progression. [33]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Pathophysiology
content: The mechanisms underlying lens opacification are multifaceted and involve several biological processes. Protein aggregation, often resulting from genetic mutations or metabolic imbalances, leads to the unfolding and clumping of crystallin proteins, thereby scattering light and impairing lens transparency. Osmotic imbalances, as seen in conditions such as diabetes and galactosemia, cause the accumulation of osmolytes within the lens, leading to cellular swelling, membrane rupture, and protein leakage. Disruption of calcium homeostasis further contributes to lens opacity by altering cell signaling and destabilizing lens proteins. [34]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Histopathology
content: The histopathology of pediatric cataracts involves the microscopic examination of lens tissue to characterize the structural changes that lead to opacification. Different cataract types exhibit distinct histopathological features, offering insight into their underlying mechanisms and informing potential treatment approaches. Pediatric cataracts commonly display disorganized and fragmented lens fibers. In healthy lenses, fibers are tightly packed and transparent. However, in cataractous lenses, the fibers may appear swollen, misaligned, or vacuolated. Aggregates of denatured or misfolded proteins, particularly crystallins, are often observed within lens fibers. These aggregates scatter light and contribute to lens opacity. Fluid-filled vacuoles are frequently seen in pediatric cataracts, especially those associated with metabolic disorders. These vacuoles arise from osmotic imbalance and lens cell damage. [36]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Histopathology
content: Genetic cataracts manifest in various forms, each with characteristic histological features. Nuclear cataracts exhibit central lens opacity with dense protein aggregation and increased compaction of lens fibers in the nucleus. Lamellar cataracts present as disk-shaped opacities involving specific layers of the lens. Histologically, these layers contain swollen and disrupted fibers with embedded protein aggregates. Posterior polar cataracts are localized to the posterior aspect of the lens and involve abnormalities of the posterior capsule and adjacent lens fibers. Histologic findings include capsular fibrosis and aberrant cellular proliferation, both of which contribute to the observed opacification. [37]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Histopathology
content: Metabolic cataracts encompass a spectrum of conditions associated with metabolic disturbances, each exhibiting distinctive pathological features. Cataracts related to galactosemia are characterized by oil droplet formations within the lens, accompanied by vacuolization, osmotic swelling of lens fibers, and deposits of galactitol. Diabetic cataracts exhibit hallmark features, including vacuolar changes, fiber swelling, and sorbitol accumulation. The osmotic effect induced by intracellular sorbitol promotes water influx into the lens, leading to opacification. Cataracts associated with Fabry disease often present with spoke-like opacities, lipid accumulation, and abnormal glycosphingolipid deposits within lens fibers. These distinct histological findings underscore the complex relationship between metabolic abnormalities and lens pathology in metabolic cataracts. [38]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Histopathology
content: Traumatic cataracts result from physical injury to the eye and are characterized by various pathological changes within the lens. Capsule rupture, subsequent fibrosis, and abnormal cell proliferation are common posttraumatic findings. Disruption of the lens capsule's integrity often results in disorganized lens fibers and the development of opacities. In some cases, calcium deposition within the lens further contributes to opacity and increases lens rigidity. These pathological alterations underscore the diverse structural and functional consequences of trauma in the development of traumatic cataracts. [40]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Histopathology
content: Certain medications can also induce cataract formation. Steroid-induced cataracts typically manifest as posterior subcapsular opacities, with histopathological findings of swollen and vacuolated lens epithelial cells. These changes result primarily from altered cellular metabolism and protein aggregation. Other drugs associated with cataract formation include miotics, chlorpromazine, and amiodarone, which produce histopathological features similar to those observed in cataract formation, including lens fiber swelling, vacuole formation, and protein aggregation. [41]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Histopathology
content: Key histopathological techniques include light microscopy, electron microscopy, and immunohistochemistry. Light microscopy of stained lens tissue sections reveals structural changes in lens fibers, protein aggregates, and cellular abnormalities. Electron microscopy offers detailed views of subcellular structures, enabling the observation of crystallin protein aggregates, membrane disruptions, and intracellular vacuoles. Immunohistochemistry detects specific proteins and cellular markers, aiding the identification of genetic mutations and metabolic disturbances that contribute to cataract formation. [42]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Toxicokinetics
content: Pediatric cataract is not primarily a toxicological disease. However, several etiologies—particularly metabolic, drug-induced, infectious, and environmental exposures—exhibit mechanisms analogous to toxicokinetics, including the absorption, distribution, metabolism, and accumulation of harmful substances or metabolic by-products that ultimately result in lens opacification. In this context, the term “toxicokinetics” in pediatric cataract describes how specific toxins, metabolites, or drugs reach the lens, interact with lens proteins, and induce structural changes that lead to cataract formation. [44]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Toxicokinetics -- General Principles of Toxicokinetics in Pediatric Cataract Formation
content: The pediatric lens is more metabolically active, osmotically vulnerable, and biochemically sensitive than the adult lens, allowing toxic insults to produce cataracts more rapidly and with greater severity in children. Key pathogenic mechanisms include intralenticular accumulation of metabolites or toxins; oxidative stress–mediated damage to crystallin proteins; disruption of osmotic balance, with consequent lens hydration changes; impairment of enzymatic pathways essential for lens transparency; and direct deposition of drugs or toxins, leading to protein denaturation. [45]

content: Several major causes of pediatric cataract share a common pathophysiologic framework in which harmful substances or energy sources enter the ocular environment, persist within lens tissues, and disrupt normal lens architecture.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Toxicokinetics -- Toxicokinetics in Major Etiological Categories
content: Metabolic disorders represent the etiological category most closely aligned with true toxicokinetic mechanisms in pediatric cataract formation. In galactosemia caused by GALT deficiency, galactitol acts as the primary toxic agent. Dietary galactose is absorbed but cannot be metabolized via normal metabolic pathways, leading to its preferential conversion to galactitol via aldose reductase. Galactitol accumulates within lens fibers, producing osmotic swelling, fiber rupture, and the characteristic “oil droplet” cataract. Cataract formation may occur within days to weeks of birth and remains reversible in early stages with prompt dietary galactose restriction. [46]

content: Drug-induced pediatric cataracts also demonstrate toxicokinetic behavior. Systemic or topical corticosteroids alter lens epithelial cell gene expression and promote oxidative damage with protein aggregation, resulting in posterior subcapsular cataract formation. Steroids readily cross the blood–aqueous barrier, and chronic exposure increases intralenticular deposition. Chlorpromazine binds directly to lens proteins, leading to pigment deposition and brown discoloration. Amiodarone, although rarely used in pediatric populations, induces granular lens deposits through drug accumulation. [49]

content: In children, the lens exhibits higher permeability, increasing susceptibility to toxins and harmful metabolites. A less mature blood–aqueous barrier permits drugs and metabolic by-products to enter the lens more readily. Rapid cellular turnover within the pediatric lens facilitates faster accumulation of structural damage. In metabolic disorders, systemic accumulation of toxic metabolites is accompanied by intralenticular deposition, which further accelerates cataract formation. [52]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Toxicokinetics -- Elimination and Reversibility
content: Elimination and reversibility of pediatric cataracts depend on the underlying etiology and duration of exposure. Cataracts associated with early galactosemia may reverse following cessation of galactitol exposure through dietary galactose restriction. Diabetes-related cataracts may demonstrate partial improvement with adequate glycemic control. In contrast, radiation- or steroid-induced, congenital TORCH-related, and longstanding metabolic cataracts are generally irreversible due to permanent structural damage to lens fibers and epithelial cells. [53] [54]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- History and Physical
content: Pediatric cataract evaluation requires a meticulous approach that integrates a comprehensive history, a thorough ocular examination, and a systemic assessment. This multifaceted process is essential to identify potential underlying causes and associated ocular or systemic conditions. History-taking should elicit key details such as age of onset, symptom duration, antenatal and perinatal events (including maternal infections, exposures, and birth complications), developmental milestones, and behavioral signs of visual dysfunction (eg, inability to catch objects, frequent falls, photophobia). The evaluation should also include any history suggestive of systemic abnormalities, trauma, prior treatment or surgery, and family history of congenital or developmental cataracts or consanguinity. [55] A history of ocular trauma or systemic steroid use is also important.

content: A detailed physical examination is equally important. The pediatric clinician should assess for systemic or genetic associations through careful inspection. For instance, head circumference measurement is particularly relevant in cases of congenital cataracts, as certain syndromes, such as trisomy 21 and Hallermann-Streiff-Francois, Lowe (oculocerebrorenal), Cri-du-chat (5p deletion), Nance-Horan, and Edward syndromes, may present with both cataracts and abnormal head size. [56]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- History and Physical
content: Reviewing family photos can be helpful when the exact onset of cataracts is unclear. Early cataracts that develop during critical periods of ocular and visual system maturation may be associated with a poorer prognosis. [57] Examination of the eyes of family members, particularly parents and siblings, may reveal undiagnosed lenticular changes suggestive of inherited causes. Autosomal dominant inheritance is the most common pattern, although X-linked recessive transmission can also occur, as seen in conditions such as Lowe and Nance-Horan syndromes. [58] [59]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- History and Physical
content: A comprehensive ocular examination is essential for the assessment of pediatric cataract. Visual acuity testing should be tailored to the child's developmental level. In preverbal children, assessment tools may include the Bruckner test, cover test, resistance to occlusion of the better eye, monocular fixation, fixation preference, vertical prism test, forced-choice preferential looking, Teller acuity cards, optokinetic nystagmus, and pattern visual evoked potential. [60] [61] The Bruckner test, performed using a direct ophthalmoscope, enables simultaneous visualization of the red reflex in both eyes. This technique can detect anisometropia or unequal refractive power. In strabismus, the deviated eye typically shows a lighter red reflex than the fixating eye. Similarly, in anisometropia, one eye may display a brighter reflex than the other.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- History and Physical
content: Verbal children undergo a multifaceted assessment of visual acuity. Detection acuity testing, using tools such as the Catford drum test and the Standardized Tests for Young Children and Retardates (STYCAR) graded ball test, evaluates the ability to perceive light or motion. [62] Recognition acuity testing assesses the ability to identify specific visual stimuli. This modality includes direction recognition using the Landolt C or Snellen E tests, letter identification with Snellen charts or high-contrast optotype visual acuity tests, and picture recognition with tools such as Allen picture cards or Domino charts.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- History and Physical
content: Ocular motility evaluation assesses for strabismus and nystagmus, which should be specifically examined in children. These findings may represent early signs of pediatric cataracts and may indicate potential visual impairment. Strabismus commonly occurs with unilateral cataract and typically develops after significant visual loss has already occurred. Congenital sensory nystagmus is frequently associated with pediatric cataracts. The presence of either strabismus or nystagmus suggests that the cataracts are visually significant. [67] [68] [69]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- History and Physical
content: IOP measurement, performed with a tonometer, helps rule out glaucoma associated with congenital rubella syndrome. [70] Pupillary reaction testing provides a rough assessment of optic nerve head function. Direct and indirect ophthalmoscopy are used to evaluate for associated vitreous or posterior segment abnormalities, such as vitreous hemorrhage, persistent fetal vasculature, fundal coloboma, and optic or macular hypoplasia. Visually significant cataracts are typically centrally or posteriorly located and measure more than 3 mm in diameter. These cataracts often result in visual acuity of 20/60 or worse, reduced contrast sensitivity, increased glare, impaired stereoacuity, and associated strabismus or nystagmus. [71] [72]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- History and Physical -- Examination of The Red Reflex
content: Medical professionals caring for children, especially newborns and neonates, must be proficient in performing the red reflex test. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends that red reflex testing be performed in all neonates and at all routine well-child visits and healthcare appointments. title: Pediatric Cataract -- Evaluation
content: The evaluation of pediatric cataract requires a systematic, time-sensitive, and interprofessional approach. Early diagnosis is critical, as visual deprivation in the first months of life may lead to irreversible amblyopia. The evaluation aims to determine cataract characteristics, including type, density, location, and laterality; assess the impact on the visual axis; identify associated ocular abnormalities; and detect underlying systemic, genetic, or metabolic causes. In addition, the assessment includes determining the timing of intervention and surgical candidacy. Both the AAPOS and the Royal College of Ophthalmologists (UK) emphasize early examination and prompt intervention for visually significant cataracts. The initial assessment relies on a thorough history and a comprehensive eye examination to identify systemic associations and ocular comorbidities. These findings inform subsequent investigations and management decisions.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Evaluation -- Imaging
content: B-scan ultrasonography is required when the fundus is not visible. This modality can exclude posterior segment pathologies that may mimic congenital cataracts, such as retinoblastoma, persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous, Coats disease, retinopathy of prematurity with retrolental fibroplasia, organized vitreous hemorrhage, congenital falciform folds, ocular toxocariasis, and retinal hamartomas. [80] [81] The AAO Pediatric Cataract Guidelines recommend performing B-scan ultrasonography before cataract surgery if the posterior pole cannot be visualized.

[82] [83] These measurements are required for IOL power calculation; pediatric formulas such as the Sanders-Retzlaff-Kraff/Theoretical or Holladay 1 are recommended, with particular caution in children younger than 2 years. title: Pediatric Cataract -- Evaluation -- Imaging
content: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is useful when media clarity permits. OCT detects macular hypoplasia, as in albinism or aniridia, aids in prognostication of visual outcomes, and evaluates epiretinal membranes or foveal development. [85] Keratometry, typically performed with handheld keratometers, requires the child’s cooperation to obtain accurate readings. A standard K value of 43.00 D may be used if the child is uncooperative. [86] Magnetic resonance imaging or computed tomography is recommended when persistent fetal vasculature or retinoblastoma is suspected, as these modalities provide detailed visualization of the brain and orbits.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Evaluation -- Genetic Analysis
content: Genetic testing is indicated for bilateral cataracts without metabolic or infectious causes, a positive family history, syndromic features, or associated ocular anomalies. Evaluation options include chromosomal microarray, targeted gene panels encompassing crystallin genes and connexins, such as GJA8 and MIP , and whole-exome sequencing in complex cases. [94] AAPOS and the Royal College recommend genetic evaluation for all cases of bilateral congenital cataracts, particularly when no definitive metabolic or infectious etiology is identified.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Evaluation -- Interprofessional Assessment
content: Additional evaluation considerations include consultations with various specialists. A pediatrician assesses systemic health, coordinates care, and evaluates for systemic signs, including growth retardation; cardiac abnormalities (eg, rubella); hearing loss (TORCH); musculoskeletal abnormalities (eg, Marfan syndrome); and renal disorders (eg, Lowe syndrome). [95] A geneticist should be consulted when hereditary conditions are suspected, providing genetic analysis and counseling. An endocrinologist may be involved when metabolic disorders that affect ocular health are suspected to ensure targeted management. [96] Neurology and developmental assessment are indicated for syndromes associated with neurological deficits, such as Down syndrome or congenital infections. [97]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Evaluation -- Interprofessional Assessment
content: Evaluation of surgical candidacy involves determining the visual significance of the cataract. Indicators for early surgery, according to AAPOS guidelines, include a central opacity measuring at least 3 mm, posterior cataracts involving the visual axis, a dense unilateral cataract, the presence of associated strabismus or nystagmus, and loss of fixation behavior. [98] Preoperative assessment for pediatric cataracts requires a comprehensive anesthetic evaluation, particularly for infants and children with comorbidities, to ensure fitness for anesthesia. The preoperative workup also includes measurement of IOP, axial length, and keratometry values, assessment for potential IOL implantation, and evaluation for persistent fetal vasculature or zonular weakness, which may influence the surgical plan.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Evaluation -- Interprofessional Assessment
content: Following diagnosis, follow-up testing is essential and includes amblyopia assessment in unilateral or asymmetric cataracts to determine the need for patching or penalization postsurgery, IOP monitoring to detect steroid-induced or angle anomaly–related glaucoma, and postoperative imaging with ultrasound or OCT for posterior segment evaluation, with repeat biometry performed in growing children if future surgery is anticipated. [99] Managing pediatric cataracts demands an interprofessional approach that integrates clinical, laboratory, and imaging assessments. Adherence to national and international guidelines helps standardize diagnosis and management, improving outcomes. Early detection and thorough evaluation are critical to preventing long-term visual impairment and enhancing the quality of life for affected children.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Evaluation -- National and International Recommendations for Pediatric Cataract Management
content: National and international guidelines emphasize early detection and timely management of pediatric cataracts. The AAO and the AAPOS recommend universal ABR screening in the newborn period, with urgent evaluation of any abnormal reflex. Surgery is advised before 6 to 8 weeks for bilateral visually significant cataracts and before 4 to 6 weeks for unilateral cataracts, with lifelong follow-up due to the risk of glaucoma and refractive changes. The Royal College of Ophthalmologists similarly emphasizes early screening at 6 to 8 weeks, recommends genetic evaluation for all cases of bilateral congenital cataracts, and underscores interprofessional care. The World Health Organization Vision 2020 Initiative focuses on early detection and referral in resource-limited settings and advocates training primary health workers in red reflex testing. [100]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Treatment / Management
content: Managing pediatric cataracts requires a coordinated effort among ophthalmologists, pediatricians, anesthesiologists, counselors, parents, and other family members. Treatment options may be medical or surgical.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Treatment / Management -- Medical Management
content: Medical management includes amblyopia therapy, such as patching the better-seeing eye to stimulate use of the amblyopic eye or using atropine drops to blur vision in the dominant eye as an alternative. [101] Refractive correction is achieved through glasses or contact lenses to address residual refractive errors after surgery. Bifocals or multifocals may be needed for near-vision tasks. [102] Low vision aids, including magnifiers and telescopic lenses, can enhance visual function in children with significant visual impairment. [103] In cases of partial or nonamblyogenic cataracts, 2.5% phenylephrine may be used to achieve mydriasis and permit vision through the nonopacified area. Optical iridectomy, though now obsolete, served a similar purpose by allowing light to pass through a clear zone of the lens. [104]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Treatment / Management -- Surgery
content: Surgical indications include any visually significant lens opacity, cataracts associated with visual acuity of 20/60 or worse, cases where the optic disc is not visible on indirect ophthalmoscopy, and central cataracts measuring at least 3 mm in size. Other indications include posterior subcapsular and nuclear cataracts, bilateral involvement, and cataracts accompanied by strabismus or nystagmus. [105] [106] Before surgery, family members must be counseled about the expected visual prognosis, the available treatment options, and the importance of regular follow-up. Postoperative visual rehabilitation and adherence to amblyopia therapy, when indicated, are essential components of care.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Treatment / Management -- Surgery
content: Surgery should be performed promptly for visually significant cataracts, ideally within a few weeks after birth, to prevent amblyopia. Surgical planning is more favorable for children older than 4, as ocular development is largely complete, and the risk of postoperative complications is lower. Unilateral cataracts are typically operated on between 4 and 6 weeks of age. For bilateral cases, the recommended interval is 6 to 8 weeks, with the second eye ideally treated within 2 weeks of the first. In bilateral cataract surgery performed within the first year of life, long-term visual acuity at 5 years is not significantly affected by the exact timing of surgery. However, earlier intervention, preferably before 2 months, correlates with better visual outcomes in unilateral cases. [107]

content: Despite these benefits, early cataract surgery is associated with a higher risk of glaucoma, particularly in unilateral cases. Thus, some surgeons may opt to delay the procedure slightly to balance visual and safety outcomes, accepting a modest reduction in visual acuity. General anesthesia with continuous monitoring of vital parameters is preferred for pediatric cataract surgery. A trained anesthesiology team and interprofessional support are essential, given the unique physiological and surgical needs of children. The type of surgery and its associated challenges have evolved significantly. Modern techniques, such as phacoaspiration with IOL implantation, have largely replaced older methods, such as discission. In 1959, Choyce and Binkhorst were the first to implant a monocular IOL in a child.

content: Pediatric cataract surgery differs considerably from adult surgery and presents distinct intraoperative challenges. Low scleral rigidity complicates incision construction and wound closure. content: Accurate IOL power calculation is crucial for achieving optimal refractive outcomes after surgery in children. However, this process poses significant challenges, particularly in accounting for the child's age and axial length. Biometry and keratometry measurements may vary depending on the instruments and techniques used. Studies have shown that the Sanders-Retzlaff-Kraff/Theoretical and Holladay 2 formulas yield the lowest predictive error among current IOL power formulas. Ongoing research is developing improved formulas to enhance the accuracy of IOL calculations in pediatric patients.

content: "Emmetropisation" refers to the postnatal adjustment of 3 primary ocular parameters—axial length, corneal curvature, and lenticular power—toward adult values as the child matures. A progressive myopic shift is expected as axial length increases with ocular growth. Therefore, the initial refractive target after IOL implantation is hypermetropia. title: Pediatric Cataract -- Treatment / Management -- National and International Guidelines
content: National and international guidelines provide comprehensive recommendations for the detection and management of pediatric cataracts. The AAP recommends performing red reflex examinations at every well-child visit beginning at birth, with immediate referral to a pediatric ophthalmologist if an abnormal red reflex is identified. The AAO emphasizes early detection and timely treatment, particularly in infants with visually significant cataracts. The AAO also recommends genetic counseling and appropriate genetic testing for families with a history of pediatric cataracts.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Differential Diagnosis -- Distinguishing Between Leukocoria Mimics and Cataracts
content: Leukocoria in children requires ruling out pediatric cataract mimics with life-threatening potential. Key mimics, clinical clues, and rule-out methods are explained below. Corneal opacities, including sclerocornea, Peters anomaly, corneal dystrophies, and congenital glaucoma-related edema, may mimic pediatric cataracts by producing a white pupillary reflex. Distinguishing features include corneal clouding, enlarged corneal diameter as seen in glaucoma, and Haab striae, which may be evaluated through slit-lamp examination, corneal diameter measurement, and IOP testing. Persistent fetal vasculature may also present with leukocoria resembling cataract, with associated microphthalmia, a stalk behind the lens, and a retrolental membrane. Diagnosis is confirmed using B-scan ultrasonography and dilated fundus examination.

content: Retinoblastoma, a life-threatening condition, may be mistaken for cataract due to leukocoria but is differentiated by strabismus and the presence of a calcified intraocular mass, requiring urgent evaluation with ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging, or computed tomography. Coats disease typically presents with unilateral leukocoria, accompanied by telangiectatic retinal vessels and exudation, which may be identified through fundus examination and fluorescein angiography. Retinal detachment, whether congenital or traumatic, may mimic a pediatric cataract by producing a white reflex or a reduced red reflex. Key distinguishing features include an elevated or folded retinal surface, which can be confirmed by B-scan ultrasonography. Toxocariasis typically presents with a white pupillary reflex; however, focal granuloma and vitreous inflammation help distinguish it, with enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), fundus examination, and ultrasound serving as confirmatory tools.

Albinism may present with a reduced red reflex or light scattering, resembling a mild cataract. Transillumination defects and nystagmus, confirmed with OCT demonstrating foveal hypoplasia, distinguish the condition. Vitreous hemorrhage opacifies the visual axis, similar to a cataract, and is suspected from a history of trauma and a hazy pupil, with B-scan ultrasonography aiding diagnosis.

Distinguishing features include cells, flare, and keratic precipitates, and the condition can be diagnosed by slit-lamp examination and inflammatory laboratory tests.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Pertinent Studies and Ongoing Trials
content: Pediatric cataract is primarily a surgical, developmental, and genetic condition rather than a pharmacologic disease. The evidence base derives from large multicenter cohort studies, population-based trials, genetic and metabolic research, and long-term outcome studies of surgical techniques. International guidelines from AAPOS, AAO, the Royal College, and WHO also inform management. A limited number of ongoing interventional trials focus on IOL design, amblyopia therapy, and postoperative care. Evidence does not support radiation therapy. [143]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Pertinent Studies and Ongoing Trials -- Key Pertinent Studies Influencing Current Practice
content: Key studies have shaped current pediatric cataract management. The IATS, a landmark multicenter randomized controlled trial, compared primary IOL implantation with aphakia corrected using contact lenses in infants aged 1 to 6 months with unilateral congenital cataract. The study found no significant difference in visual acuity at 4.5 years. However, primary IOL implantation in infants younger than 6 months was associated with higher complication and reoperation rates, whereas aphakia with contact lenses led to fewer adverse events. These results prompted AAPOS and AAO to recommend caution when implanting IOLs in infants younger than 6 months, emphasizing individualized decision-making. [144]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Pertinent Studies and Ongoing Trials -- Key Pertinent Studies Influencing Current Practice
content: Observational cohort studies on early surgery timing consistently demonstrate that dense bilateral cataracts should ideally be removed by 6 to 8 weeks of age, while unilateral cataracts should typically be excised by 4 to 6 weeks. Delays beyond 10 weeks are associated with severe amblyopia, consistent with the “sensitive period” of visual development, as shown by Birch, Lambert, and colleagues. [145] Longitudinal studies on postoperative glaucoma, including reports from Wang, Beck, and the IATS glaucoma follow-up, indicate that 30% to 40% of children develop glaucoma after pediatric cataract surgery. The risk is higher in infants operated on before 6 months, in eyes with microphthalmia, persistent fetal vasculature, or juvenile-onset open-angle glaucoma patterns, underscoring the necessity for lifelong IOP monitoring. title: Pediatric Cataract -- Pertinent Studies and Ongoing Trials -- Key Pertinent Studies Influencing Current Practice
content: Although not specific to cataract management, amblyopia treatment trials from the Amblyopia Treatment Studies conducted by the Pediatric Eye Disease Investigator Group provide the evidence base for postoperative visual rehabilitation. These findings support the international recommendation for genetic testing in bilateral cataracts. [147]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Pertinent Studies and Ongoing Trials -- Studies on Surgical Techniques and Outcomes
content: Studies on surgical techniques and outcomes further inform contemporary pediatric cataract management. Investigations by Wilson, Trivedi, Vasavada, and Dahan demonstrate that combining posterior capsulotomy with anterior vitrectomy in children younger than 6 years significantly reduces VAO and decreases the need for secondary interventions, establishing this combined approach as a standard technique worldwide in this age group. [149] Multiple studies evaluating IOL power calculation highlight the challenges unique to pediatric eyes. Formulas such as Sanders-Retzlaff-Kraff/Theoretical and Holladay 1 are commonly used in older children, while Holladay 2 and Barrett Universal II are emerging as more accurate options in pediatric populations. Large corneal curvature and shorter axial length complicate refractive prediction, leading many surgeons to intentionally leave residual undercorrection to accommodate the anticipated myopic shift associated with rapid ocular growth. [150]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Pertinent Studies and Ongoing Trials -- Ongoing Clinical Trials and Research Areas
content: Ongoing research continues to refine pediatric cataract management across surgical, genetic, and rehabilitative domains. Clinical trials evaluating next-generation adjustable IOLs, including light-adjustable and modular types, focus on the feasibility of postoperative refractive adjustment, long-term safety and biocompatibility, and the potential to reduce long-term anisometropia. Gene therapy trials remain in early-phase investigation, targeting gene replacement for crystallin mutations and correction of connexin-related cataract pathways. These approaches remain experimental and have not yet entered clinical practice. [152]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Pertinent Studies and Ongoing Trials -- Ongoing Clinical Trials and Research Areas
content: Pharmacologic strategies aimed at preventing secondary cataract formation after surgery are under investigation, including agents such as mammalian target of rapamycin inhibitors, transforming growth factor–beta inhibitors, and capsular bag–surface modifying compounds, with the primary goal of reducing posterior capsule opacification. [154] Long-term neurodevelopmental outcome studies follow children after cataract surgery to assess cognitive development, binocular vision potential, and the comparative impact of early versus delayed intervention. Findings from these studies continue to inform and refine evidence-based guidelines regarding the optimal timing of surgery. [155]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Treatment Planning
content: Treatment planning for pediatric cataract is complex and must account for timing, laterality, cataract type, ocular comorbidities, systemic disorders, and long-term visual rehabilitation needs. Given the heightened sensitivity of visual development in early childhood, pediatric cataract management is time-critical and interprofessional, requiring coordination among pediatric ophthalmologists, anesthesiologists, optometrists, geneticists, and pediatricians. This planning is guided by clearly defined objectives that prioritize visual development and long-term ocular health. Primary goals include early restoration of a clear visual axis, prevention or treatment of amblyopia, achievement of appropriate refractive correction, management of coexisting ocular or systemic conditions, and establishment of lifelong follow-up to monitor for complications such as glaucoma.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Treatment Planning
content: The visual significance of the cataract determines the necessity for treatment. Intervention is indicated when lens opacity obscures the visual axis, a central cataract measures at least 3 mm, or posterior cataracts involve the visual axis and impair central vision. Additional indications include strabismus or nystagmus and rapid cataract progression. According to AAPOS guidelines, any visually significant cataract identified during infancy warrants urgent referral and evaluation for surgical management. The timing of surgery is a critical component of treatment planning because the developing visual system is highly susceptible to deprivation. Delayed intervention during sensitive periods of visual maturation substantially increases the risk of irreversible amblyopia, underscoring the importance of prompt, age-appropriate surgical decision-making.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Treatment Planning
content: Surgical timing in pediatric cataract is determined by laterality, density, etiology, and the risk of visual deprivation. Dense unilateral congenital cataracts require surgical removal at approximately 4 to 6 weeks of age, while dense bilateral congenital cataracts are optimally treated between 6 and 8 weeks of age to minimize amblyogenic risk. Partial or developmental cataracts are managed based on visual axis clarity, rate of progression, and measurable visual function rather than strict age thresholds. Traumatic cataracts require individualized timing, guided by the degree of inflammation, capsular integrity, and the risk of lens-induced glaucoma. Delays beyond 10 to 12 weeks of age are associated with permanent visual deprivation and poor long-term visual outcomes.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Treatment Planning
content: Preoperative planning for pediatric cataract surgery requires a detailed ocular evaluation, precise biometric assessment, and careful procedural selection to minimize complications and optimize long-term visual outcomes. Comprehensive ocular assessment includes a slit-lamp examination to evaluate lens opacity and to identify associated anomalies, such as posterior synechiae, PFV, aniridia, coloboma, and microphthalmia. IOP measurement is essential to detect preexisting or secondary glaucoma, which may influence surgical timing and technique.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Treatment Planning
content: Biometric evaluation is mandatory when IOL implantation is under consideration. Required measurements include axial length, keratometry, and anterior chamber depth. These parameters are critical for IOL power calculation and surgical planning, particularly in eyes with abnormal growth patterns. Several factors influence the decision to implant an IOL. Age represents the most critical determinant, given the rapid ocular growth in infancy. Ocular size must be carefully assessed, as microphthalmia is associated with an increased risk of intraoperative and postoperative complications. The presence of ocular comorbidities, including persistent fetal vasculature or uveitis, may contraindicate primary implantation. Surgeon experience and family capacity to maintain contact lens therapy also influence decision-making. [156] Evidence-based guidance from the IATS recommends avoiding primary IOL implantation in infants younger than 6 months. Between 6 months and 2 years of age, the decision should be individualized. Beyond 2 years of age, primary IOL implantation is considered standard practice.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Treatment Planning
content: The preferred surgical approach for pediatric cataract includes lens aspiration followed by anterior capsulotomy, performed manually or using a vitrector. Complete irrigation–aspiration of lens material is required. Posterior capsulotomy with anterior vitrectomy is routinely performed and is mandatory in children 6 years of age or younger to reduce the risk of posterior capsule opacification (PCO). IOL implantation is performed when indicated. [157]

content: Preferred IOLs include single-piece acrylic lenses, with 3-piece designs reserved for cases requiring sulcus placement. Refractive targeting typically favors mild hyperopia in younger children to compensate for the anticipated myopic shift associated with ocular growth. Contraindications to IOL implantation include severe microphthalmia, active uveitis, aniridia with inadequate capsular support, and uncontrolled glaucoma. [158]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Treatment Planning
content: Immediate postoperative management of pediatric cataract involves anti-inflammatory therapy with frequent topical steroids and cycloplegics to control inflammation and improve comfort. Topical broad-spectrum antibiotics are administered for 1 week to prevent infection, and IOP monitoring is essential given the risk of early postoperative glaucoma. [159] Optical rehabilitation depends on lens status: aphakic eyes require contact lenses or aphakic spectacles, whereas pseudophakic eyes need age-appropriate spectacles for residual refractive error. Occlusion therapy is indicated for unilateral cataracts, with frequency and duration guided by the ATS, and atropine penalization may serve as an alternative in selected cases.

Annual reviews continue lifelong to monitor for glaucoma, PCO, refractive changes, and secondary membrane formation. [160] Complication surveillance includes early- and late-onset glaucoma, visual axis opacity (VAO), IOL decentration, strabismus, and recurrence of amblyopia. [161]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Toxicity and Adverse Effect Management
content: Although systemic chemotherapy or radiation is not used to treat pediatric cataract, "toxicity and adverse effect management" refers to complications related to surgical intervention, adverse effects of postoperative medications, issues arising from implantable devices such as IOL, and long-term consequences of early ocular surgery in infants. This section outlines potential adverse events and presents evidence-based strategies for their management. [164]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Toxicity and Adverse Effect Management -- Surgical Toxicities and Adverse Effects
content: Surgical toxicities and adverse effects in pediatric cataract include intraoperative complications such as posterior capsule rupture caused by excessive aspiration, weak capsule, or persistent fetal vasculature (PFV), managed with anterior vitrectomy and modified IOL placement if necessary. Iris trauma, often resulting from a small pupil or synechiae, is addressed using iris hooks or sphincterotomy and postoperative topical steroids. Zonular dialysis, due to congenital weakness or trauma, requires a capsular tension ring or modified IOL fixation. Hyphema from instrumental trauma is managed with observation, topical steroids, and, in rare cases, anterior chamber washout.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Toxicity and Adverse Effect Management -- Postoperative Toxicities and Their Management
content: Postoperative toxicities after pediatric cataract surgery encompass inflammation, secondary glaucoma, VAO, infection, and IOL-related complications. Children exhibit robust postoperative inflammation, characterized by fibrinous uveitis, posterior synechiae, and membrane formation, and are managed with intensive topical steroids (initially every 1–2 hours), cycloplegics to prevent synechiae, subconjunctival steroids in severe cases, and adjunctive nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. [165] Secondary glaucoma affects 15% to 40% of children postoperatively, with the highest risk when surgery occurs before 6 months of age, presenting as open-angle, angle-closure, or pupillary block glaucoma. Lifelong IOP surveillance, age-appropriate gonioscopy, and optic nerve evaluation are essential. Management includes topical IOP-lowering agents (eg, β-blockers and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors; avoid prostaglandins in infants) and surgical interventions, such as trabeculotomy, goniotomy, or valve implantation, for refractory cases. [166]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Toxicity and Adverse Effect Management -- Postoperative Toxicities and Their Management
content: VAO, the most common adverse outcome in young children, arises from lens epithelial cell proliferation and is prevented by primary posterior capsulotomy combined with anterior vitrectomy in children younger than 6. Secondary treatment includes yttrium aluminum garnet capsulotomy in older children or surgical membranectomy if laser application is not feasible. [167] Endophthalmitis is rare but sight-threatening, with risk factors including wound leak or intraoperative contamination. Management requires immediate intravitreal antibiotics, vitrectomy in severe cases, and prophylaxis with intracameral and postoperative topical antibiotics.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Toxicity and Adverse Effect Management -- Postoperative Toxicities and Their Management
content: IOL-related toxicities include decentration or dislocation, particularly in cases of zonular weakness, as seen in Marfan syndrome or PFV, and are managed by repositioning, scleral fixation, or IOL exchange. Refractive surprise, or myopic shift, results from rapid eye growth and is managed with regular refraction, spectacles, contact lenses, or adjustment of the IOL target. Rarely, uveitis–glaucoma–hyphema syndrome can develop from iris chafing and is managed with IOL repositioning or exchange, along with steroid therapy.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Toxicity and Adverse Effect Management -- Medication-Related Toxicities
content: Medication-related toxicities in pediatric cataract care include steroid-induced glaucoma, atropine-related systemic effects, and contact lens–related complications in aphakia. Children are often steroid responders, necessitating IOP measurement at every visit while on steroids. Management involves gradual tapering, switching to weaker agents such as loteprednol, and adding IOP-lowering drops when indicated. [168] Atropine, used for amblyopia therapy and postoperative comfort, may cause flushing, fever, tachycardia, and central nervous system effects in small infants. Management requires the minimal effective dose and parental education on signs of systemic toxicity. Use of aphakic contact lenses can lead to keratitis, hypoxia, and corneal neovascularization. Strict hygiene, high oxygen-permeability lenses, and regular corneal evaluation mitigate these risks. [169]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Toxicity and Adverse Effect Management -- Long-Term Adverse Outcomes
content: Amblyopia typically develops in nearly all cases of unilateral cataract unless the cataract is aggressively treated. Management includes patching in accordance with ATS protocols, atropine penalization when appropriate, and consistent follow-up to detect recurrence. Strabismus may arise from visual deprivation or postoperative ocular imbalance. Management consists of optical correction, amblyopia therapy, and strabismus surgery once ocular alignment stabilizes. Late-onset glaucoma can develop years to decades after surgery. Lifelong follow-up is essential, with early intervention using IOP-lowering medications or surgical procedures when indicated. [170]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Toxicity and Adverse Effect Management -- Family Education as Part of Toxicity Prevention
content: Family education plays a critical role in preventing treatment-related toxicities. Emphasis should be placed on strict adherence to eye drops, patching regimens, and scheduled follow-up visits. Families must be informed of signs of infection, including ocular pain, redness, and photophobia. Education should also address the long-term risk of glaucoma and provide instruction on proper contact lens hygiene for aphakic infants.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Staging -- Morphological Classification
content: Nuclear cataract: Located in the central nucleus of the lens; often congenital and can significantly impair vision if dense Cortical cataract: Affects the cortex, or outer layer, of the lens; may progress slowly, with the degree of visual impairment depending on the extent and location of the opacities Posterior subcapsular cataract: Positioned at the back of the lens, just anterior to the posterior capsule; often causes glare and difficulty with bright light, markedly affecting near vision Lamellar (zonular) cataract: Involves a specific layer or zone of the lens (see Image . Pediatric Cataract, Zonular Type); dense, centrally located opacities can cause substantial visual impairment Anterior polar cataract: Located on the anterior surface of the lens capsule; typically small and may not considerably impair vision unless the cataract enlarges [171]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Staging -- Severity Based on Density and Extent
content: Pediatric cataracts may also be staged based on severity, which helps guide clinical decisions. Classification into mild, moderate, or severe reflects the degree of visual impact and informs the timing of treatment. Mild cataract: Small lens opacities that do not substantially interfere with vision; managed conservatively with regular monitoring Moderate cataract: More extensive opacities that cause noticeable visual impairment; may require surgical intervention if vision is functionally compromised Severe cataract: Dense opacities that markedly impair vision or cause blindness; prompt surgical management is typically necessary to restore vision and reduce the risk of amblyopia [172] Effective management of pediatric cataracts depends on accurate assessment of severity. Early intervention in moderate-to-severe cases is critical for optimal visual outcomes.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Staging -- Impact on Vision
content: Assessing the functional impact of a cataract on a child’s vision is crucial. This classification supports early identification of cases requiring surgical management versus observation. Visually insignificant cataract: Lens opacity that does not strikingly impair vision or causes only minor visual disturbances. Regular follow-up is necessary to monitor for progression. Visually significant cataract: Leads to marked visual impairment that affects daily function and visual development. Requires timely surgical intervention to prevent amblyopia and optimize visual outcomes. [173]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Staging -- Location Relative to the Visual Axis
content: The location of a pediatric cataract within the lens directly influences visual development and the severity of visual disturbance. Cataracts are commonly classified as central or peripheral based on their location. Central cataract: Situated along the central visual axis; more likely to interfere with vision and visual development, often necessitating early intervention Peripheral cataract: Located outside the central visual axis; may not significantly impair vision unless the cataract progresses centrally This classification assists clinicians in prioritizing cases for surgical referral; central cataracts pose a higher risk and should be addressed more urgently

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Staging -- Laterality
content: The distinction between unilateral and bilateral cataracts guides prognosis and therapeutic approach. Early identification is essential to minimize the risk of long-term visual impairment. Unilateral cataract: Involves only 1 eye; carries a higher risk of amblyopia due to unequal visual input, necessitating early diagnosis and prompt intervention Bilateral cataracts: Involve both eyes; can cause symmetrical visual impairment and typically require coordinated surgical and rehabilitative management [174]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Prognosis
content: Numerous factors influence the final visual outcome in children with pediatric cataracts. Visually significant cataracts produce blurred retinal images, which disrupt the development of visual pathways and cortical connections in the occipital lobe. With improved understanding and surgical techniques, early removal of visually significant cataracts is now recommended to prevent sensory deprivation amblyopia. Unilateral cataracts are more amblyogenic than bilateral cases, underscoring the importance of early surgery within the first few weeks to months of life.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Prognosis
content: The timing of diagnosis plays a critical role in determining visual prognosis—the earlier the diagnosis and treatment, the better the outcome. Ocular conditions such as microcornea, corneal opacities, glaucoma, intraocular inflammation, posterior segment abnormalities, and ocular motility disorders (eg, unsteady fixation, strabismus, or nystagmus) are associated with poorer postsurgical outcomes. [175] The prognosis of pediatric cataracts depends largely on the timing of diagnosis and intervention, the presence of systemic or genetic conditions, and the effective management of complications. Early detection and prompt treatment are essential for optimizing long-term visual outcomes.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Prognosis
content: Children diagnosed and treated within the first few weeks to months of life generally have a better prognosis. Early intervention prevents amblyopia and supports normal visual development. In contrast, delays in diagnosis and treatment can lead to permanent visual impairment, including amblyopia and associated developmental deficits, underscoring the importance of timely detection. [176] Patients with isolated cataracts, ie, those not associated with ocular or systemic abnormalities, tend to have a more favorable prognosis when treated early. Cataracts linked to genetic syndromes or metabolic disorders present additional management challenges and often carry a more guarded prognosis due to the presence of concurrent health issues.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Prognosis
content: Modern surgical techniques, including IOL implantation, have markedly improved outcomes in pediatric cataract management. Successful cataract extraction, followed by effective visual rehabilitation, frequently results in favorable visual outcomes. Postoperative care plays a crucial role. Proper management of complications such as PCO and secondary glaucoma, along with regular follow-up and adherence to treatment, considerably enhances long-term prognosis. [177]

Ongoing support through occupational therapy and visual skills training can further improve outcomes, particularly in children with developmental delays secondary to visual impairment.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Complications
content: As with other intraocular procedures, pediatric cataract surgery carries inherent risks that may necessitate further treatment. These complications can compromise visual outcomes if not promptly identified and managed. Visual axis opacity (VAO) is a potential cause of amblyopia following cataract surgery. [179] The condition is inevitable if the posterior capsule is left intact. VAO arises from the proliferation, migration, and metaplasia of lens epithelial cells extending from the equator to the posterior capsule. Even after a well-executed posterior capsulotomy, secondary membranes and media opacities may still form. An intact hyaloid face can serve as a scaffold for epithelial cell migration and transformation.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Complications
content: One of the most influential factors in VAO development is the patient's age at the time of surgery. Other contributing factors include the type of cataract, the presence of associated ocular abnormalities (eg, PHPV, uveitis), aphakic or pseudophakic status, IOL type, the size of the capsular opening, and the completeness of cortical cleanup. Adequate posterior capsulotomy, with or without vitrectomy, is essential to prevent VAO. In-the-bag IOL implantation further reduces the risk. If the child is cooperative, Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy may be used to clear the opacification. Surgical intervention, such as membranectomy, may be necessary to restore visual axis clarity in cases of dense or thick VAO. [180]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Complications
content: Glaucoma develops in 10% to 25% of cases following pediatric cataract surgery. [181] Open-angle glaucoma is more common, although pupillary block glaucoma can also occur. Medical therapy is typically the initial approach. However, surgical management becomes necessary in refractory cases. Surgical options include trabeculectomy, implantation of glaucoma drainage devices, and cyclodestructive procedures. [182]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Complications
content: Postoperative anterior uveitis is more common in children than in adults due to heightened tissue reactivity. No-touch surgical techniques and in-the-bag IOL fixation help reduce the incidence of this condition. Frequent postoperative administration of topical steroids or posterior sub-Tenon injection of triamcinolone acetonide may be necessary. Dense fibrinous exudates and postoperative miosis occur in some cases. Mydriatic agents, such as atropine or subconjunctival injection of mydricaine, may be used to prevent synechiae formation and achieve adequate mydriasis.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Complications
content: Postoperative IOL-related complications may include surface deposits, synechiae, pupillary capture, opacification, and decentration. Additional IOL-related issues may involve incorrect IOL power calculation, dislocation, or intraocular inflammation. These complications highlight the importance of accurate IOL power estimation and meticulous surgical technique. Surgical repositioning or replacement may be required in cases of IOL dislocation or significant malfunction.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Complications
content: Amblyopia is a developmental condition characterized by reduced visual acuity, often due to unequal visual input. This condition frequently arises in children with cataracts, particularly when unilateral or dense. Early diagnosis and intervention are essential to prevent long-term visual impairment. Treatment strategies include occlusion therapy (patching of the dominant eye), pharmacologic penalization with atropine, and refractive correction using glasses or contact lenses. [183]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Complications
content: PCO is the most common postoperative complication following pediatric cataract surgery. The lens capsule becomes cloudy, resulting in decreased visual acuity. Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy is typically performed to restore a clear visual axis and improve vision. [184] Strabismus may develop in children with cataracts due to unequal visual input to the brain, which disrupts binocular vision and leads to ocular misalignment. Management options include corrective glasses, patching, orthoptic exercises, and surgical realignment of the extraocular muscles. [185]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Complications
content: Postoperative inflammation and infection, including endophthalmitis, are serious complications of cataract surgery in children. Prophylactic antibiotics and anti-inflammatory agents are administered postoperatively to minimize risk. Rapid recognition and aggressive treatment of infection are essential to prevent irreversible vision loss. [186] Retinal detachment, though rare, is a potentially sight-threatening complication characterized by the separation of the neurosensory retina from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium. Immediate surgical repair is necessary to reattach the retina and preserve visual function. [187]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Complications
content: Postoperative refractive errors, such as myopia (nearsightedness) and hyperopia (farsightedness), may occur after pediatric cataract surgery and may affect visual acuity. Corrective lenses, ie, glasses or contact lenses, are prescribed to address these errors and achieve optimal visual outcomes. [188] Phthisis bulbi is a condition in which the eye becomes shrunken and nonfunctional due to severe intraocular damage or chronic inflammation. Preventive strategies include timely and appropriate management of postoperative complications. Enucleation may be necessary in advanced or painful cases. [189]

content: Corneal opacification may develop as a result of chronic inflammation or infection, reducing corneal transparency and impairing vision. Continuous monitoring and aggressive management of underlying causes are essential. Corneal transplantation may be required to restore visual function in advanced cases.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Complications
content: Other complications may include cystoid macular edema, retinal detachment, endophthalmitis, heterochromia, corneal decompensation, bullous keratopathy, astigmatism, and unexpected postoperative refractive outcomes. [190] Monitoring and managing morbidities linked to pediatric cataracts are essential for achieving optimal visual outcomes. An interprofessional approach that emphasizes regular follow-up, timely intervention, and comprehensive care is crucial for effectively addressing these complications and improving the quality of life in children with cataracts.
