title: Pediatric Cataract -- Complications -- Other Clinical Implications
content: The morbidity associated with pediatric cataracts extends beyond lens opacity and includes developmental, surgical, and lifelong sequelae. Untreated pediatric cataract leads to disease-related complications driven by visual deprivation during the critical period of visual development. Amblyopia is the most common consequence and is often irreversible without timely intervention, while early bilateral deprivation may result in nystagmus with poor visual prognosis. Sensory asymmetry frequently leads to strabismus, resulting in functional impairment and cosmetic concerns. Prolonged deprivation contributes to delayed visual maturation and reduced visual potential. Late presentation or lack of intervention may lead to irreversible blindness, representing a major public health burden.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Complications -- Other Clinical Implications
content: Preoperative and diagnostic complications include misdiagnosis of leukocoria, most critically due to failure to exclude retinoblastoma or PFV. Missed retinoblastoma carries life-threatening consequences, underscoring the need for urgent and thorough evaluation of any abnormal red reflex before proceeding with cataract management. During pediatric cataract surgery, posterior capsule rupture may occur because of a thin capsule or excessive surgical manipulation, increasing the risk of VAO and secondary glaucoma. Zonular dialysis, resulting from congenital zonular weakness or trauma, compromises capsular support and predisposes to IOL instability. Hyphema may develop from intraoperative iris trauma and can lead to secondary inflammation or glaucoma. Vitreous loss, most often associated with capsular rupture, is linked to higher rates of postoperative complications and more complex postoperative management.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Complications -- Other Clinical Implications
content: In the early postoperative period, excessive inflammation commonly occurs because of the robust inflammatory response characteristic of pediatric eyes, leading to synechiae formation and secondary membranes. VAO, driven by the proliferation of residual lens epithelial cells, represents the most frequent postoperative complication in children. Early-onset secondary glaucoma may develop as a result of angle damage or pupillary block and constitutes a sight-threatening condition with lifelong implications. Endophthalmitis, although rare, is a vision-threatening postoperative emergency related to surgical infection. Wound leaks from poor healing may result in hypotony and increase the risk of infection.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Complications -- Other Clinical Implications
content: Late postoperative complications include secondary glaucoma with delayed onset, attributed to angle recession and altered aqueous dynamics, which may manifest years after surgery. IOL decentration or dislocation may occur due to capsular contraction or zonular weakness, leading to visual disturbance and, in some cases, the need for reoperation. Refractive surprise or progressive myopic shift results from continued ocular growth in children and necessitates frequent refractive reassessment and optical adjustment. PCO develops from residual lens epithelial cell proliferation and causes reduced vision, while retinal detachment, although rare, arises from vitreoretinal traction and represents a vision-threatening complication.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Complications -- Other Clinical Implications
content: Optical and rehabilitation-related complications significantly influence long-term outcomes. Poor compliance with contact lens wear, often related to caregiver burden or cost, contributes to suboptimal visual rehabilitation. Spectacle intolerance, commonly due to anisometropia or magnification effects, impairs binocular vision. Recurrent amblyopia may develop in the setting of inconsistent patching and typically requires prolonged and closely supervised therapy.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Complications -- Other Clinical Implications
content: Medication-related complications include steroid-induced glaucoma, reflecting heightened reminder responsiveness in children and necessitating close IOP monitoring, as well as steroid-induced cataract progression associated with prolonged corticosteroid exposure and worsening lens opacity. Atropine toxicity may occur due to systemic absorption, presenting with fever, flushing, and central nervous system effects. Systemic and long-term consequences extend beyond ocular morbidity. The psychosocial impact of childhood visual disability contributes to educational difficulties and social challenges. A substantial economic burden results from lifelong treatment, frequent follow-up, and rehabilitative needs, affecting both family resources and broader societal support systems.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: Early visual rehabilitation of children with pediatric cataracts is as crucial as early diagnosis and treatment. Rehabilitation reduces the incidence of amblyopia, strabismus, and poor fusion. Some options for visual rehabilitation in these children are spectacles, contact lenses, IOLs, epikeratophakia, low vision aids, and amblyopia therapy. Parents should be counseled on the importance of regular follow-up and routine refraction, as refractive changes are frequent during ocular growth.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: Children younger than 2 require aphakic glasses or contact lenses for visual rehabilitation after cataract surgery until secondary IOL implantation is considered. Aphakic glasses are typically recommended for bilateral aphakia. However, the use of these vision aids has declined with advancements in surgical techniques and the increasing prevalence of primary IOL implantation. The goal of aphakia management is to provide appropriate optical correction following cataract extraction to enable symmetrical stimulation of the visual system during its critical period of development. title: Pediatric Cataract -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: Spectacles are the earliest form of aphakia treatment. Aphakic glasses with bifocal addition remain the most commonly used option for visual rehabilitation in children with bilateral aphakia. These devices are affordable and accessible, and they do not cause ocular discomfort or require direct contact with the eye's surface. However, these visual aids are limited by considerable weight and bulk, restricted peripheral vision, optical distortions—including the jack-in-the-box phenomenon, pincushion effect, and ring scotoma—and potential aggravation of nystagmus. In unilateral cases, spectacles are less suitable because anisometropia and aniseikonia can lead to diplopia and amblyopia, which may result in permanent suppression and anomalous retinal correspondence.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: Contact lenses are the most effective optical correction for postoperative aphakia. These lenses should be worn during waking hours and removed at night. Contact lenses are superior to spectacles in both unilateral and bilateral aphakia, offering a wider visual field, reduced glare and spherical aberrations, improved binocularity, and better cosmetic appearance. However, poor tolerance, cost, and nonadherence are common challenges, particularly among younger children. Chronic eye disease and ocular surface disorders are contraindications to the procedure.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: Available options include polymethylmethacrylate, rigid gas-permeable, silicone elastomer, and hydrogel lenses. Extended-wear lenses are often preferred, though their use is limited by complications such as giant papillary conjunctivitis, neovascularization, corneal abrasions, and infectious keratitis, making daily-wear lenses the safer alternative. Children older than 2 with primary IOL implantation still require adequate visual rehabilitation after surgery. Spectacles or contact lenses are prescribed after appropriate refraction. [192]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care -- Amblyopia Treatment
content: Deprivational amblyopia is highly prevalent in pediatric cataracts, particularly during the critical period of visual development in the first 2 months of life, due to unequal visual input between the eyes. Unilateral cataracts generally produce more severe amblyopia than bilateral cases, necessitating prompt surgical intervention. Early initiation of amblyopia therapy is essential for visual rehabilitation, with occlusion therapy—patching the better eye per ATS protocols—serving as the primary modality. Pharmacologic penalization with atropine provides an alternative in selected cases. Ensuring adherence to therapy is often challenging, making caregiver counseling and consistent follow-up critical for effective treatment. Patients require reevaluation every 2 weeks to assess visual improvement and monitor for reversal of amblyopia. [193]

Other commonly used devices include bifocals, hand magnifiers, stand magnifiers, electronic magnifiers, telescopes, and computer-based closed-circuit televisions.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care -- Immediate phase
content: Immediate postoperative management (days 0–7) requires vigilant monitoring for early complications, including infection, IOP elevation, inflammation, and wound integrity issues. Intensive topical corticosteroids, initially administered hourly and then tapered, control the robust pediatric inflammatory response. Cycloplegic agents, such as atropine or cyclopentolate, reduce pain and prevent posterior synechiae formation. Broad-spectrum topical antibiotics are essential to prevent postoperative infection.

Wound integrity should be assessed by slit-lamp examination to identify complications, such as wound leakage or iris prolapse. Consistent administration of prescribed medications and proactive monitoring are critical to ensuring optimal recovery and maintaining postoperative comfort. [194]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care -- Early phase
content: During the early postoperative period (weeks 1–6), corticosteroids are tapered gradually based on the degree of inflammation to prevent rebound uveitis. Slit-lamp and red reflex examinations allow early detection of VAO. Initial refraction is performed once the cornea stabilizes to enable timely optical correction. Serial IOP measurements monitor for steroid-induced or aphakic glaucoma.

Periodic refraction addresses myopic shift and ensures optimal optical correction.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care -- Long-term care
content: Lifelong glaucoma surveillance (1 year after surgery onward) involves regular IOP measurement and optic nerve evaluation, as glaucoma may develop years after surgery. Secondary procedures, including YAG capsulotomy or membranectomy, restore visual axis clarity when needed. Strabismus surgery corrects ocular misalignment, improving binocularity and cosmesis. Low-vision rehabilitation with visual aids and training enhances functional vision.

IOP should also be measured routinely to detect the onset of postoperative glaucoma, a known complication. [195]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care -- Visual rehabilitation
content: Corrective lenses are essential for addressing residual refractive errors and optimizing visual development. Infants with aphakia require contact lenses, while aphakic spectacles may be used when appropriate to restore a focused retinal image. Children with pseudophakia benefit from age-appropriate spectacles to correct residual refractive error and optimize visual acuity. High-index lenses or contact lenses are recommended for anisometropia to improve binocular vision. Amblyopia treatment remains crucial, with occlusion therapy, such as patching the dominant eye, enhancing the weaker eye’s function, and supporting binocular development. [196]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Consultations
content: A pediatric cataract may occur in isolation or as part of a systemic disease involving other organ systems, such as the cardiac, renal, or central nervous systems. Effective management of pediatric cataracts often necessitates an interprofessional approach, involving consultations with various healthcare professionals to ensure comprehensive care. A pediatric ophthalmologist (or cornea specialist) plays a central role in diagnosing, performing surgery, and managing postoperative care for pediatric cataracts. The expertise of these providers in pediatric-specific surgical techniques is critical for achieving successful visual rehabilitation. Consultation with a pediatric ophthalmologist should be initiated promptly upon suspicion or diagnosis to facilitate timely intervention and prevent long-term visual impairment. [200]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Consultations
content: The pediatrician (eg, neonatologist) is essential for overall health evaluation, including the exclusion of systemic comorbidities and gross congenital anomalies that may contribute to cataract development. Pediatricians coordinate with specialists to manage these conditions and ensure integrated care. Routine pediatric examinations should include screening for ocular abnormalities, with timely referral to a pediatric ophthalmologist if cataract signs are detected. If cataracts are suspected to be hereditary, a genetic counselor can provide necessary guidance on recurrence risk in future pregnancies and facilitate genetic testing. Consultation should be considered when a family history of cataracts or a suspected genetic syndrome is present. [201]

An anesthesia consultation should occur well before surgery to plan safe anesthetic administration during the procedure. [202]

An infectious disease specialist is warranted when TORCH or other congenital infections are suspected, with responsibilities including serologic testing and infection management to limit disease progression and systemic morbidity. Optometrists (or refraction specialists) assist in the postoperative care of children with cataracts by prescribing corrective lenses and monitoring visual development. These professionals play a vital role in ongoing visual rehabilitation. Regular postoperative consultations should be scheduled to ensure proper correction and to detect any changes in vision. [203]

content: Emotional and psychological support for the child and family is essential, primarily when cataracts significantly affect the child’s quality of life. Social workers or psychologists can provide counseling and connect families with support resources. Consultation should be considered early in the course of treatment to ensure comprehensive support. A pediatric neurologist should be consulted when developmental delay or central nervous system anomalies are present, to facilitate formal neurological assessment and identify associated neurodevelopmental disorders. Engagement with public health services or nongovernmental organizations is particularly valuable for children from rural or underserved populations, as it supports awareness initiatives and provides financial assistance to reduce preventable childhood blindness.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Deterrence and Patient Education -- Deterrence
content: Protecting maternal and infant health during pregnancy and early childhood is critical for preventing pediatric cataracts. Mitigative strategies should address modifiable risk factors that contribute to cataract development in newborns and young children. Encouraging maternal vaccination against infections known to cause congenital cataracts, such as rubella, and minimizing exposure to pathogens like T gondii and CMV can reduce the risk of intrauterine infection. Adequate maternal nutrition, particularly intake of vitamin A, folic acid, and ω-3 fatty acids, supports normal fetal eye development. Regular prenatal checkups allow early identification and management of maternal or fetal issues that may affect ocular development. [205]

Genetic counseling is recommended for families with a history of pediatric cataracts or known genetic disorders to guide risk assessment and early detection strategies. [206] Metabolic disorders such as galactosemia, diabetes, and hypocalcemia should be included in newborn screening protocols, as these conditions may lead to cataract formation if left untreated. Children with identified systemic or metabolic diseases require ongoing ophthalmic monitoring to detect and manage cataracts at the earliest stage. [207] Reducing the incidence of pediatric cataracts requires an integrated approach targeting prenatal care, infection prevention, maternal nutrition, genetic assessment, and early detection and management of systemic conditions.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Pearls and Other Issues -- Disposition
content: Comprehensive preoperative evaluation is essential and should include a detailed ocular examination, assessment of visual acuity, and evaluation for any underlying systemic conditions. The timing of surgery is critical. Surgical intervention is recommended between 6 and 8 weeks of age for bilateral significant cataracts and between 4 and 6 weeks for unilateral cataracts. Appropriate anesthesia and diligent postoperative care are vital to minimizing complications. Regular follow-up is necessary to monitor for conditions such as glaucoma, PCO, and amblyopia. Visual rehabilitation, using glasses, contact lenses, or patching, is crucial to achieve optimal visual outcomes. [211]

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Pearls and Other Issues -- Pitfalls
content: Delayed diagnosis of pediatric cataracts can result in irreversible visual impairment. Routine check-ups must include vigilant screening to facilitate early detection. Inadequate postoperative management, particularly failure to address complications such as IOP elevation, uveitis, or secondary cataract formation, may compromise visual outcomes. Close postoperative monitoring is essential. Noncompliance with follow-up visits and prescribed treatments, including corrective lenses and occlusion therapy, significantly increases the risk of poor visual development and amblyopia. Parental education is necessary to ensure adherence.

title: Pediatric Cataract -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Pediatric cataracts are often first identified in primary care settings, typically when concerned parents observe leukocoria, ocular misalignment, or nystagmus. Primary healthcare clinicians play a critical role in promptly referring these children to specialized centers equipped to manage pediatric cataracts. content: Effective management of pediatric cataracts demands specialized expertise and a coordinated strategy. Pediatric ophthalmologists must be adept at diagnosing and surgically treating congenital and developmental cataracts. A well-executed plan emphasizing early intervention and continuous follow-up is critical to preventing long-term visual disability.

Responsibilities also include maintaining confidentiality, delivering equitable care, and addressing ethical challenges, such as surgical timing and managing cases with limited prognostic value.
